idiom_name: sealed interface (unexported marker method) + type switch + exhaustiveness linter
implementation_notes: Go has no sum types, so the closed set is simulated: declare an interface whose method set contains an unexported marker method (type Shape interface { isShape() }) and implement it on the variants declared in the same package - only that package can satisfy the interface, because no other package can name the unexported method - then dispatch with a type switch (switch v := s.(type) { case *Circle: ... }). The compiler cannot see the variant set, so exhaustiveness comes from a linter that recognises the sealing convention (go-check-sumtype with a //sumtype:decl marker, gounion, sumlint under go vet) plus a default arm that panics, and because an interface value can be nil that default must also handle nil. The interface-plus-implementation split replaces the classic Visitor; keep it (or plain polymorphic methods) when the set is open or third parties must add variants.
pitfalls: An interface value can be nil, so a type switch without a default arm silently returns zero values for nil independent of the variant set.
A default arm that returns a fallback disables coverage checking: go-check-sumtype needs -default-signifies-exhaustive=false unless the default only panics.
The sealing trick limits the set to one package by construction, and the marker method shows up in the interface's method set, so cross-package extension is impossible - deliberate, but binding.
